Few counterpoints:

  • I think there's probably more to this than the article is letting on: If the company was genuinely profitable before the pump and dump, there'd be no reason for it to crash afterwards. Even if all the investors panic-sold their shares, and someone unscrupulous got their hands on them, a healthy company is still more valuable than an asset-stripped one.

  • The core idea of having employers be pension and healthcare providers is a very very bad one. If anything happens to the company for any reason you not only lose your income, you lose your savings too. There's also a weird situation with some public employers where they can take away your pension as a punishment. It would make much more sense to just pay employees the money that would have been spent on premiums and let them buy their own healthcare/make their own investments.

  • Asset stripping dying companies might seem heartless, but it's a useful economic activity. If the tools and inventory a company is sitting on would be more valuable in someone else's hands, then it's the market's job to get them to that person. If you don't want to be exposed to that outcome, don't publically trade your company.

  • Pump and dumps are a good example of fence paradox. People assume the STC has their back, and unfair practices will be punished, so they don't do their due diligence and fall for scams. If the scammers are connected, they're shit out of luck and they lose their money. If not they might get some of it back. If the STC didn't exist they'd probably be more careful in the first place.
